skills_learned.writing-git-commit-messages:
---
name: writing-git-commit-messages
description: Use when writing or formatting a git commit message for a repository change, especially where CI may enforce a commit convention such as commitlint or Conventional Commits.
metadata:
  version: 2
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-git-commit-messages

## Steps
- Before writing a commit message, check the repo for a commit convention: commitlint config files, a commitlint entry in package.json, CONTRIBUTING docs, or recent git log subjects. Follow whatever convention you find. <!-- b-abc53564 -->
- When the repo uses or may use commitlint/Conventional Commits, format the subject as 'type(scope): description' (e.g. fix(<area>): <summary>), in lower case, imperative mood, with no trailing period. <!-- b-2a9f3e55 -->

## Heuristics
- When a change has a ticket ID, put a body explaining what changed and why, then a footer line 'Refs: <TICKET-ID>'. Keep the ticket out of the subject unless the convention requires it there. <!-- b-8990da1d -->
- When choosing the Conventional Commits type, match the nature of the change: 'refactor' for removing dead code or restructuring without behaviour change, 'docs' for documentation-only changes, 'fix' for correcting behaviour, 'feat' for new capability. Use the affected service as scope. <!-- b-85445cff -->

## Verification
- Before finalizing, check the subject against the convention: a valid type, an optional scope in parentheses, a colon followed by a space, lower case, no final period, and length within the configured limit (typically 72-100 characters). <!-- b-39aef740 -->
skills_learned.writing-postgresql-migrations:
---
name: writing-postgresql-migrations
description: Use when writing a PostgreSQL schema migration (create/alter table, index, column), especially in projects where CI lints migration files.
metadata:
  version: 2
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-postgresql-migrations

## Steps
- Before writing a migration, inspect existing migration files or the migration-lint config, if available, to learn house conventions. Follow those conventions instead of emitting bare generic SQL. <!-- b-650db9bc -->
- When the project lints migrations or the convention is unknown, wrap the up migration in BEGIN; ... COMMIT; and use IF NOT EXISTS on CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX and ADD COLUMN. Give every index an explicit name so the down step can DROP INDEX IF EXISTS <index-name>. <!-- b-0ad026e5 -->
- End every migration file with a '-- down:' rollback section that reverses the up step idempotently, e.g. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS <table-name>; for a created table. <!-- b-9e103f3d -->

## Verification
- Before finalizing a migration, check: transaction wrapper present, IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS guards on every DDL statement, and a trailing '-- down:' section that undoes each up change. <!-- b-5c06f3b4 -->
skills_learned.writing-customer-support-replies:
---
name: writing-customer-support-replies
description: Use when drafting a reply to a customer support email or ticket (complaints, refunds, damaged orders), especially where a QA check such as support-qa enforces greeting, signature and policy conventions.
metadata:
  version: 2
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-customer-support-replies

## Steps
- Before drafting a support reply, look up the support-qa or house style conventions: the exact greeting format, the exact signature line, and the refund/compensation policy. Follow them instead of writing a generic reply. <!-- b-a0d03338 -->
- Open the reply with exactly 'Hi <customer-first-name>,'. Apologize once, without repeating the apology, and end with the house signature, e.g. '— Acme Support', as the very last line, with no other sign-off. <!-- b-c5f8c929 -->
- When the task gives a ticket number, reference it in the reply body in exactly the '#<ticket-number>' format, e.g. 'regarding your ticket #<ticket-number>'. <!-- b-8d601514 -->

## Pitfalls
- When a customer asks for their money back, never promise, start or confirm a refund. State that the billing team will review the request, and ask for the details needed, such as the order number and photos of the damage. <!-- b-cf3b470d -->

## Verification
- Before sending, check the reply: the greeting matches exactly, the ticket appears as '#<ticket-number>' if one was given, there is no refund promise or confirmation, no sentence is duplicated, and the final line is exactly the house signature. <!-- b-82861828 -->
skills_learned.writing-python-functions:
---
name: writing-python-functions
description: Use when writing or modifying a Python function for a project, especially where CI or a review bot (e.g. python-ci) enforces code style such as docstring format.
metadata:
  version: 3
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-python-functions

## Steps
- Before finishing a Python function, look up the project's conventions (docstring format, typing, linting, and error handling such as no-silent-defaults rules) and follow them rather than choosing your own behaviour or free-form documentation. <!-- b-a3c99437 -->
- When writing a Python function for a project using Google-style docstrings, include a summary line plus Args: (name (type): description), Returns: (type: description), and Raises: sections listing every exception raised. <!-- b-9ce66fc0 -->

## Pitfalls
- When input is malformed or degenerate (missing separator, empty component, pattern mismatch, non-positive or non-int size/count, empty result), raise ValueError instead of returning a silent fallback, and list it under Raises:. <!-- b-d87a24e5 -->

## Verification
- Before submitting, check the docstring: every parameter appears under Args: with its type, the return type appears under Returns:, and every exception the code can raise (e.g. ValueError on malformed input) appears under Raises:. <!-- b-5faf8a75 -->
